A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Data Taggants research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

before.justification: v1 reports original ImageNet1k experiments measuring classification accuracy, key detection, stealthiness, and transfer across architectures and training recipes, including appendix results.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds comparisons with established ownership-verification methods, detector analyses, and dataset-modification experiments.

M1.justification: Both versions use random image/label keys, class-matched per-key gradient matching, differentiable augmentations, LPIPS, random restarts, and binomial detection. v2 explains the relationship to Witches' Brew more explicitly, but the proposed procedure and final optimization objective remain unchanged.

E1.justification: ImageNet1k image classification remains the sole benchmark and task. v2 adds ownership-verification scenarios where Bob incorporates additional classes or subsamples Alice's data before adding other classes (Section 4.3 and Table 10). These extend the dataset-use conditions tested beyond v1's shared-dataset scenario.

E2.justification: v2 Table 1 adds actual comparisons against BW–Sleeper Agent, BW–BadNets, and Data Isotopes. Naive Canary and Transparency remain elsewhere. The DBSCAN comparison also loses the Transparency and no-perceptual-loss control curves shown in v1 Figure 4.

E3.justification: The added ownership-verification comparison reports TPR/FPR using a specified k=10, tau=0.1 detection rule. New experiments introduce detector and backdoor-test threshold sweeps, half-class dataset construction, and 20% subsampling. DBSCAN's stated feature source changes from a clean model in v1 to a model trained on signed data in v2. Existing training recipes and budgets remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 replaces the fixed-operating-point poisoning-defense table with ROC analyses, revises the DBSCAN analysis, and removes the separate cleanlab k-NN OOD analysis. It adds backdoor-test margin sensitivity in Figure 8 and dataset-modification robustness in Table 10. The perceptual-loss/weight-decay comparison, architecture-transfer tests, and 800-epoch check were already present in v1.

E5.justification: Four random-initialization runs, standard-deviation reporting, and Fisher aggregation of taggant p-values remain. v2 additionally reports the backdoor comparators' t-test p-values across margins, with shaded variation bands in Figure 8. It does not establish an increase in repeated-run counts.

E6.justification: New Table 1 reports TPR/FPR of 1.0/0.0 for taggants, 0.0/0.0 for both backdoor baselines, and 0.53/0.20 for Data Isotopes. New Table 10 reports top-10 key accuracies of 62.5±15.0% and 72.5±9.6% under dataset modifications. Detector and margin-sensitivity results also change. Matched budget, transfer, and 800-epoch table values remain unchanged.

T1.justification: v2 Section 3.3 adds Proposition 1 and an explicit Bernoulli-to-binomial proof of expected honest-model key accuracy k/|Y|. v1 already stated the binomial distribution and tail-probability test, so this is a limited addition of formal justification rather than a new detection theorem.

C1.justification: The central claims of harmless, stealthy, statistically controlled black-box verification remain. v2 explicitly presents perceptual loss for poison crafting as a contribution and removes the conclusion's 'in favorable settings' qualification while emphasizing high detection rates and low false-positive rates.

C2.justification: v2 newly interprets existing Mixup/CutMix experiments as resistance to poisoning defenses and explains how backdoor-test margins can favor false detection of benign models. It replaces v1's untested subset/superset limitation with positive conclusions from the new dataset-modification tests. The clustering explanation and architecture-transfer limitations largely remain.

D1.justification: v2 adds a statement promising code release upon publication, without providing an implementation link, and clarifies augmentation resampling during optimization. It removes v1's approximately 150,000 GPU-hour project estimate. Hardware, per-stage timings, model sizes, augmentation settings, and training-recipe tables are retained.

R1.justification: New Appendix A.1 and Table 5 substantially expand positioning against prior ownership-verification methods and explain baseline inclusion and exclusion. Sections 2 and 3.3 expand comparisons of statistical guarantees. Added references cover dataset inference, membership-inference limitations, gradient-attack inversion, and poisoning defenses; the Stable Signature and cleanlab OOD references are removed.

P1.justification: v2 extensively rewrites the introduction, contribution list, related work, and method/detection explanations. It creates standalone limitations, ethics, and reproducibility sections and reorganizes the appendix around a new prior-work comparison section. These are substantial narrative and structural revisions beyond the added experiments.

P2.justification: v2 redraws the application and gradient-matching diagrams, annotates the objective visually, adds comparison tables and ROC/margin plots, and replaces the original defense displays. It condenses the main budget table while retaining its results in the appendix and moves the architecture stress-test table there. Existing qualitative image examples are retained.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens support for a central claim: v1 asserted superiority over backdoor watermarking without directly evaluating established DOV baselines, whereas v2 Table 1 supplies those comparisons. Table 10 also tests dataset modifications left to future work in v1, and the ROC and margin analyses improve scrutiny of detection behavior. These gains outweigh limited disclosure losses. However, v2 introduces a threshold inconsistency: with 10 keys and 1,000 classes, top-10 accuracy at least 0.1 implies about 9.6% theoretical false positives; the stated 0.4% requires at least two matching keys.
